content:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-term autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. It often affects the small joints of the hands and feet on both sides of the body. It can affect people of any adult age. Early treatment with disease-modifying medicines can control it and prevent joint damage.

How RA differs from osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis develops gradually as joints try to repair everyday wear and damage. RA is caused by the immune system. It produces more inflammation, can affect many joints at once, and can affect other parts of the body such as the lungs, eyes and heart. RA needs specialist treatment from a rheumatology team.

Symptoms

  • pain, swelling and warmth in joints, often the hands, wrists and feet
  • stiffness, especially in the morning or after resting, lasting more than 30 minutes
  • symptoms affecting the same joints on both sides
  • tiredness, sometimes severe
  • feeling generally unwell, a mild fever, or losing weight
  • firm lumps under the skin near joints (rheumatoid nodules) in some people

Symptoms often come and go, with periods of worse symptoms called flares.

Causes and risk factors

The exact cause is not known. A mix of genes and environmental factors seems to be involved. Risk factors include:

  • being female. RA is two to three times more common in women.
  • being middle-aged, though it can start at any adult age
  • a family history of RA
  • smoking, which is the strongest lifestyle risk
  • being overweight

How it is diagnosed

There is no single test. Your GP will examine your joints and may arrange:

  • blood tests for inflammation (CRP and ESR)
  • rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody tests
  • X-rays or ultrasound

Many people with RA have positive antibody tests, but not all. NICE (NG100) says that adults with persistent joint swelling should be referred urgently to rheumatology even if blood tests are normal. A rheumatologist confirms the diagnosis.

Treatment

  • DMARDs, such as methotrexate, are started as soon as possible to control the immune system.
  • Steroids may be used short-term to calm symptoms quickly.
  • Biologics and targeted medicines are used if DMARDs alone are not enough.
  • Painkillers help symptoms but do not change the disease.
  • Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and podiatry help you stay active and manage daily tasks.

Your team will check your disease activity regularly and adjust treatment until it is under control.

Possible complications

RA increases the risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and lung and eye problems. Good disease control, not smoking and regular checks reduce these risks.

Living with RA

  • stay active with a mix of aerobic, strength and flexibility exercise
  • stop smoking
  • pace yourself and plan rest
  • get your vaccinations, as some treatments make infections more likely
  • look after your mental health, as low mood is common
  • learn your flare plan and who to contact

Work and support

Many people with RA continue to work. Employers must consider reasonable adjustments, and Access to Work can help with costs. Depending on how RA affects you, benefits such as PIP may be available.

When to see your GP

See your GP if you have joint pain, swelling and stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, especially in your hands and feet. Early referral makes a real difference to the long-term outlook.

Questions to ask after diagnosis

  • How active is my RA, and what is our treatment target?
  • How long will my medicine take to work?
  • What blood tests do I need, and how often?
  • Who do I contact during a flare?
  • Can I be referred to physiotherapy or occupational therapy?

Writing your questions down before appointments helps you get the most from them.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
